21:
The advisor's body leaves the floor before his feet find it. He lands halfway down the corridor, papers wheeling after him, one shoe skidding off near the maid's bucket. The impact knocks something loose in his throat—a thin, wet sound like a cough that can't start.

He doesn't try to get up. He gets his palms flat on the stone and pushes, and his knees shake so hard the fabric of his hose shivers. His chin stays tucked, and when he speaks it's into the floor.

"Yes, Your Highness."

The maid is gone. Her bucket remains, overturned, water spreading in a dark tongue toward the wall.

The guard at the end of the corridor has turned fully around now, both hands at his sides and his back against the stone. Rook stands a few steps behind you, close to the wall, and he doesn't look at the advisor. He looks at you, the way a man looks at a fire he didn't set.

The advisor gets one foot under him, then the other, still bent low. He's trying to bow and run at the same time, and neither is working.

"Yes, Your Highness," he says again, and goes. Not down the corridor past the guard, but sideways, toward the servant's stair, one hand sliding along the wall as if the stones might hold him up. His papers stay where they fell. The shoe stays where it skidded.
22:
The sword is in your hand before the last word is out. It appears the way a drawn breath fills a chest: sudden and already complete, the blade bright as a sliver of morning off the window, and the weight of it settles into your fingers as though it had always been hanging at your hip. The corridor goes very still. The guard at the far end has stopped pretending to watch the wall. His mouth is half-open, and his hand has found the hilt of his own sword without his eyes leaving the one in yours.

Rook is still against the stone. He doesn't flinch. He doesn't reach for his knife. His hands are at his sides, and his gaze moves from the blade to your face and then to the floor. He takes a step back, not far, just enough that his shoulders meet the wall, and his knuckles crack once at his side, then twice. The sound is very loud.

He doesn't answer at once. His jaw works, the scar along it gone pale. Then he says, flat, "The gate took my name. There's a log. You want to know who let me in, ask the man at the gate."

Behind you, the advisor's shoe is still lying in the water from the overturned bucket.

Rook looks at the sword again, then at you. There's no warmth in his face at all, and no give. He stands the way a man stands in a doorway during an argument he didn't start, too far in to leave and too wary to sit.

"Half the palace knows you spent yesterday in the gardens with a creature in a dress," he says. "The other half's pretending they don't. I came to see if the king was the kind of man who'd leave a debt open or settle it."
24:
The spear leaves your hand before the last word is out. It buries itself in the stone beside Advisor's head, close enough that the ash shaft grazes his ear, and the crack of it echoes down the corridor.

Advisor's legs fold. He goes down hard, one hand scrabbling at the wall, the other still pressed to his chest as if the papers there could stop anything. His mouth works. A thin sound comes out, high and wordless. He doesn't look at the spear. He doesn't look at Rook. He looks at you, and his breath is coming in short, wet gasps.

"I'm going," he says. "Your Highness. I'm going now. Right now."

He gets one foot under himself and then the other, and his back stays flat against the wall as he half-crawls, half-runs backward. A button has come loose on his coat. His heel catches in the water and he nearly goes, and then he is through the archway and the sound of his shoes is going away at a run, uneven, slapping through the corridor's own echoes.

Behind you, the spear still stands in the wall. The tremor of the impact has gone, but a fine crack runs up from the point of it, right through the carved vinework.

And then the door at the far end of the corridor opens, and a woman comes through it.

She stops.

She is tall, square-shouldered, in a dark travelling cloak gone grey with dust along the hem. Her boots are scuffed and practical, laced high, and her legs are bare from the ankle to the knee. She carries herself like someone used to moving through rooms without being stopped. Her face is sharp and watchful, and when she takes in the corridor—the body, the head against the wall, the spear in the stone, you with the sword still in your hand—she goes very still.

A young woman lingers just behind her, half-hidden in the doorway. Her hands are white-knuckled on the frame. She is small, dark-haired, with paint flaking at the corners of her mouth, and she is looking at Rook's head with her whole face slack.

The first woman's hand goes to something at her hip, out of sight beneath the cloak.

"Three weeks I've walked for a man who's already dead," she says, and her voice is flat and hoarse, as if the dust has gotten in it too. "Which one of you killed Rook?"
